http_status: 403 on every host tested, without exception

extracted.purpose: Falsify the original researcher's central diagnostic claim that fda.gov / lilly.com / sec.gov were subject to an ORIGIN bot-block distinct from an EGRESS-policy denial affecting api.fda.gov, cms.gov, medicare.gov, hhs.gov and trumprx.gov.
extracted.webfetch_control_example_com: https://example.com/ -> HTTP 403 Forbidden. example.com serves no bot protection and does not 403 real clients. A 403 here proves the block is at the fetch layer, not at the origin.
extracted.webfetch_control_secondary_host: https://www.drugs.com/foundayo.html -> HTTP 403 Forbidden. A plain secondary aggregator also 403s, so 403 carries zero signal about the identity or policy of the target publisher.
extracted.conclusion: Both channels are closed for all hosts. There is no origin-vs-egress distinction. No primary source of any kind was retrievable by this verifier either, so the original gate's nulls stand, but its stated reasons and its remediation recommendation are wrong.
extracted.consequence_for_original_report: The original report's recommendation that 'unblocking api.fda.gov is the single highest-value remediation' is a misdiagnosis. api.fda.gov is not specially blocked; everything is. Equally, the original report's inference that a 403 on download.open.fda.gov/crl/CRL_BLA125827_20260410.pdf demonstrates that the file EXISTS is invalid, because an identical 403 is returned for example.com.
